headline: Base case is S&P 500 pullback not a trend change, but not yet ready to buy the dip — elevated risk in stocks below their moving averages
reasoning: The S&P 500 equal-weight index hit a three-month low and has been closing below the 100-day moving average for the first time since April. Rallies are being sold and buyers are coming in later to buy dips, indicating weaker price action beneath the surface. A large number of S&P 500 stocks are already down more than 20%, with only a handful of mega-cap stocks holding up the headline index. An indicator tracking the percentage of S&P 500 stocks above their 100-day moving average has dropped into the 30–42% 'reversal region', which has historically produced recoveries after mild-to-moderate corrections. McIntosh's base case is that this is a pullback rather than a trend change, but he is not yet ready to buy the dip, particularly in stocks trading below their moving averages where risk is elevated.
quote: I think our base case should be that stocks are experiencing a pullback, not a trend change. Um, so I think look, with the S&P 500, I think the play remains, as we've been discussing for months, and that is giving the incumbent trend the benefit of the doubt. That said, I'm not quite ready to buy this dip at the moment. Well, um, particularly in stocks which are below their moving averages, which is a large segment of the market, I think there is elevated risk. And and stocks need to prove themselves before before buying.

headline: S&P 500 gives appearance of broad strength — rising moving averages, within 2% of all-time high — but equal-weight S&P hit a three-month low and many constituent stocks are already down more than 20%, with mega-cap strength masking broad weakness
reasoning: The S&P 500 cap-weighted index shows rising moving averages and is within 2% of an all-time high, consistent with an ongoing bull market. However, the equal-weight S&P 500 traded at a three-month low and has had a series of closes below the 100-day moving average for the first time since April. Rallies are being sold and buyers are progressively coming in later to buy dips. Many stocks within the S&P 500 are already down more than 20%, which is hidden by the strength of a handful of mega-cap names holding up the index.
quote: I think September has lived up to its reputation for for volatility, but you wouldn't know it by looking at the S&P 500. The key index gives the appearance of a broad market strength. It has rising moving averages. It's within 2% of an all time high. The latest dip appears to be finding support. So these are all signs of an ongoing bull market. But that's not the case for most stocks. Um, the equal weight. When you think about the S&P 500 on an equal weight basis, it traded at a three month low on Wednesday. And for the first time since April, it's had a series of closes below the 100 day moving average. And we've got a situation where the rallies are being sold and buyers are progressively coming in later to buy the dips. So this is a very different price action. What we're seeing in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, in fact, many, many stocks within the S&P 500 are already experiencing bearish conditions. A large number of stocks are down by more than 20%. But that's hidden by the strength we're seeing in the big cap indices. And it's really, really the strength of those handful of mega caps which is making the difference.

headline: ASX 200 vulnerable to break below September low and retest June low (~8500); not a bear market but risk has increased and not rushing to buy the dip
reasoning: The ASX 200 has been below its 50 and 100 day moving averages for about three weeks, and the rebounds are not gaining traction. Both moving averages are declining and slanting to the downside, indicating sellers remain dominant. McIntosh sees risk that prices break below the September low and retest the June low around 8500, which would take prices to the lower end of the 12-month range. He does not think a bear market is the most likely scenario, but says the risk has increased and this is not a normal pullback to rising moving averages. He is not selling stocks without a reason but is also not rushing to buy the dip, preferring the market to prove itself before increasing risk.
quote: The outlook starting with the ASX 200. It's so far, this isn't the bounce I wanted to to see. The ASX 200 has been below its moving averages for about three weeks now, and the rebound that we've been seeing, it's not really getting very much traction at all. The other thing to note is that the moving averages continue to roll over. So I've got both the 50 and the 100 day moving averages on the chart. They're both declining and they're both stained across to the downside. The thing with weak rebounds is that they indicate that the sellers remain dominant, especially when that happens below the decline in moving averages. I think the risk now is that prices break below the September low and then retest the June low. That's around 8500. And then that would take prices to the lower end of their 12 month range. I think it's important to note, though, that this does not mean that a bear market is about to unfold. I don't think that's the most likely scenario, but I think it's important to understand that that risk has increased. And this isn't a normal pullback to rising moving averages.
